lessons.title: What crypto is
lessons.description: A ledger, a key, and a wallet: the whole idea in three minutes.

exercises.prompt: What is a blockchain, in plain terms?

options.text: A shared ledger that many computers keep in sync
A bank account that pays interest
A wallet that stores coins

exercises.explanation: A blockchain is a ledger copied across many machines, so no single party can rewrite it quietly.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Crypto assets are only useful for speculation.
exercises.explanation: They also carry payments, access, and identity use cases. Speculation is one use, not the only one.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about ownership.
parts: A crypto asset sits in a
, and control of it comes from a
exercises.explanation: The wallet holds the address; the key proves you may move what is there.

exercises.prompt: Match each key with how it should be treated.
exercises.explanation: The public address receives funds. The private key moves them, so it stays secret.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: A confirmed transaction on a public blockchain can be reversed by a bank if you ask nicely.
exercises.explanation: Confirmed transactions are final. Recovering a mistake needs the recipient to send the funds back.

exercises.prompt: Why does a blockchain keep many independent copies of the ledger?

options.text: So no single copy can be changed without the others noticing
So transactions split into smaller pieces and run faster
So the owners of coins stay hidden

exercises.explanation: Copies that must agree make a silent edit easy to detect and reject.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about sending crypto.
parts: that the network checks and adds to the
exercises.explanation: A transaction is one signed transfer. The ledger is the shared record it is written into.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: A computer that stores and checks the ledger
A batch of transactions added to the chain together

exercises.explanation: Nodes keep the network honest. Blocks group transactions into the ledger in order.

lessons.title: Wallets and keys
lessons.description: Backups, seed phrases, and the mistakes that cannot be undone.

exercises.prompt: You lose your private key and have no backup. What happens?

options.text: You lose access to that wallet
Support restores it for you
Nothing, it regenerates

exercises.explanation: Self-custody means nobody can reset your key for you. The backup is the recovery plan.

exercises.prompt: Put safe wallet setup in order.

steps.text: Open a wallet app you trust
Write the seed phrase on paper, offline
Receive a small test amount

exercises.explanation: Create, back up offline, then test with a small amount before trusting it with more.

exercises.prompt: Complete the backup rule.
exercises.explanation: Paper or metal, offline. Photos and cloud notes are easy to steal.

exercises.prompt: What do you do next?
exercises.body: A 'wallet inspector' DMs you: 'Your wallet is at risk. Send your seed phrase so I can secure it.'

options.text: Send the phrase quickly
Ignore and report the account

exercises.explanation: No legitimate service needs your seed phrase. Anyone who asks is attacking you.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Keeping your seed phrase as a screenshot on your phone is as safe as paper.
exercises.explanation: Phones sync screenshots to the cloud, and those copies can leak. Paper kept offline is safer.

exercises.prompt: A website asks you to enter your seed phrase to "recover" your funds. What is this most likely to be?

options.text: A phishing attempt
Normal account recovery
A required security update

exercises.explanation: Real wallets never ask for the seed phrase on a website. Typing it there hands the funds to whoever runs the site.

exercises.prompt: Match each wallet type with its trade-off.

right.text: Keys stay on a dedicated device offline
Connected to the internet, convenient for small amounts

exercises.explanation: Offline keys resist remote attacks. Connected wallets trade some safety for convenience.

exercises.prompt: Put these steps in order after losing a phone.

steps.text: Confirm the seed phrase backup exists
Install the same wallet app on a new device
Restore the wallet from the seed phrase

exercises.explanation: Check the backup first. Without it, the wallet cannot be restored.

lessons.title: Reading a candle
lessons.description: Open, high, low, close: what one candle tells you.

exercises.prompt: Which candle closed weakest relative to its open?

options.text: Candle 1
Candle 2
Candle 3

exercises.explanation: Candle 2 opened at 105 and closed at 92, giving up the most ground.

exercises.prompt: What do the thin wicks above and below a candle show?

options.text: The highest and lowest prices in that period
The trading fee
The number of buyers

exercises.explanation: Wicks mark the extremes reached before the period closed.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: A green candle guarantees the price will keep rising.
exercises.explanation: One candle describes the past. It never guarantees the next move.

exercises.prompt: Put a simple candle read in order.

steps.text: Note where it opened and closed
Note the high and low wicks
Compare it with the previous candle

exercises.explanation: Body, wicks, then context. A candle alone is not a signal.

exercises.prompt: What does a long upper wick usually show?

options.text: Price was pushed up, then sellers pushed it back down
The market closed at its high
Nobody traded in that period

exercises.explanation: A long upper wick shows price reached a higher level and was rejected there.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: The close of a candle is the last traded price in its time period.
exercises.explanation: Open and close are the first and last trades. High and low are the extremes reached in between.

exercises.prompt: Which candle had the largest body that closed above its open?

options.text: Candle 1
Candle 2
Candle 3

exercises.explanation: Candle 2 rose 14 points from open to close, the largest bullish body. Candle 3 closed lower.

exercises.prompt: What is the most careful reading of this candle?
exercises.body: A coin spikes to a new high and falls back within the same candle. The volume is thin.

options.text: The spike proves a strong uptrend
The rejected spike is a weak signal, so wait for confirmation

exercises.explanation: A rejected spike on thin volume tells you little. The next candles confirm or deny the move.

lessons.title: Support and resistance
lessons.description: The price levels where buyers and sellers keep showing up.

exercises.prompt: What is support?

options.text: A price area where buyers have repeatedly stepped in
A guarantee that price cannot fall further
The highest price of the year

exercises.explanation: Support is a zone of past demand, not a floor that cannot break.

exercises.prompt: Match each level with its usual nickname.
exercises.explanation: Support sits below price, resistance above. Either can break.

exercises.prompt: Price bounced near which level three times?
exercises.explanation: Each low lands near 100, which is the support zone being tested.

exercises.prompt: What is the calmer choice?
exercises.body: Price just closed below a support level you have watched for weeks. A friend says it is 'free money' to buy now.

options.text: Buy immediately
Wait for confirmation before acting

exercises.explanation: Broken support often becomes resistance. Waiting for confirmation costs less than guessing.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: A support level that breaks often turns into resistance.
exercises.explanation: After price falls through support, sellers often defend the old level when price climbs back to it.

exercises.prompt: Which situation best describes resistance?

options.text: Price repeatedly stalls under the same ceiling
Price has no history at any level
Price moves randomly with no reaction to any level

exercises.explanation: Resistance is a level where selling repeatedly stops the price from rising.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about price levels.
parts: A level gets stronger the more often price
exercises.explanation: Repeated reactions mark a level. A decisive break is the moment to reassess the trade.

exercises.prompt: Put a support-based plan in order.

steps.text: Mark the support level on the chart
Wait for price to test the level and hold
Set your stop just below the level

exercises.explanation: Identify the level, wait for confirmation, then define the loss you accept.

lessons.title: Dollar-cost averaging
lessons.description: Buying on a schedule instead of guessing the perfect moment.

exercises.prompt: You follow a fixed weekly plan. What is the right action at each price shown?
exercises.explanation: A fixed plan buys the same amount on schedule. Price swings do not change the rule.

exercises.prompt: What does dollar-cost averaging mean?

options.text: Buying a fixed amount on a fixed schedule
Buying only after a big drop
Selling everything at the high

exercises.explanation: DCA spreads purchases over time, so one entry price does not decide your outcome.

exercises.prompt: You risk 1% of a 1000 unit balance with entry at 100 and stop at 95. What position size should you take?
exercises.explanation: Risk is 10. Each unit risks 5, so buy 2 units: a 200 position.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Dollar-cost averaging removes the risk of losing money.
exercises.explanation: It reduces timing risk only. The asset can still fall.

exercises.prompt: Why does dollar-cost averaging reduce timing risk?

options.text: It spreads purchases over time, so you do not buy everything at one peak
It guarantees a higher average return
It removes all losses

exercises.explanation: Spreading purchases lowers the chance that all your money goes in at the worst moment.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Pausing purchases whenever price drops is part of a good DCA plan.
exercises.explanation: The plan buys on schedule regardless of price. Stopping on dips defeats its purpose.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about the plan.
exercises.explanation: The rule, not the price on the day, decides each purchase.

exercises.prompt: You risk 2% of a 5000 unit balance with entry at 50 and stop at 45. What position size should you take?
exercises.explanation: Risk is 100. Each unit risks 5, so buy 20 units: a 1000 position.

lessons.title: Time in the market
lessons.description: Why patience and compounding beat reaction.

exercises.prompt: Why does time in the market usually beat timing the market?

options.text: Missing the best days hurts long-run returns
Fees disappear after a year
Prices only rise over time

exercises.explanation: A few strong days carry a lot of the long-run return, and they are impossible to predict.

exercises.prompt: Complete the compounding sentence.
exercises.explanation: Returns earning returns needs time, and time needs patience.

exercises.prompt: What do you do?
exercises.body: Your portfolio drops 20% in a week. A headline says the market is finished.

options.text: Sell everything today
Re-read your plan and stick to it

exercises.explanation: A written plan made before the drop is calmer than a headline made during it.

exercises.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
exercises.explanation: Volatility is movement. Drawdown measures how far you are from a high.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Compounding works mainly because returns earn returns over time.
exercises.explanation: Gains that stay invested produce their own gains, so the effect grows with time.

exercises.prompt: A coin drops 30% in a week. Which response fits a long-term plan?

options.text: Sell everything to stop the pain
Check the plan and keep buying on schedule if the reason you own it still holds
Double the position to win back losses quickly

exercises.explanation: A plan is judged against its reasons, not against the latest price move.

exercises.prompt: Put a patient review routine in order.

steps.text: Write down why you own the asset
Check the plan once a month, not every hour
Adjust only if the reason has changed

exercises.explanation: Start from the reason. Frequent checks invite reactions; changes need a changed reason.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea with what it describes.

right.text: Growth that builds on earlier gains
Trying to buy at the exact bottom

exercises.explanation: Compounding rewards staying invested. Timing requires predicting moves, which is hard to do reliably.

lessons.title: Position sizing
lessons.description: Decide how much you can lose before you decide what to buy.

exercises.prompt: You risk 2% of a 2000 unit balance with entry at 50 and stop at 45. What position size should you take?
exercises.explanation: Risk is 40. Each unit risks 5, so 8 units: a 400 position.

exercises.prompt: What is a common risk limit for a single beginner trade?

options.text: 1-2% of the account
25% of the account
Whatever the chart looks like

exercises.explanation: Small fixed risk keeps a normal losing streak survivable.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Position size should be chosen before entering a trade.
exercises.explanation: Size comes from the stop distance and the risk budget, not from excitement.

exercises.prompt: Put the trade plan in order.

steps.text: Define where the idea is wrong
Size the position from that stop
Place the order

exercises.explanation: Invalidation first, size second, order last.

exercises.prompt: What is the first step in position sizing?

options.text: Decide the most you can lose on one trade
Pick the asset with the highest potential gain
Choose the entry price from the latest post

exercises.explanation: The allowed loss sets the size. The size should never be set by the upside you hope for.

exercises.prompt: You risk 0.5% of a 2000 unit balance with entry at 20 and stop at 18. What position size should you take?
exercises.explanation: Risk is 10. Each unit risks 2, so buy 5 units: a 100 position.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Putting more of your balance into one trade reduces your risk when the setup looks strong.
exercises.explanation: A bigger position raises the loss per trade. A strong-looking setup does not cancel that.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about risk per unit.
parts: Risk per unit is the gap between entry and
. Divide the allowed loss by it.
exercises.explanation: Position size = risk amount ÷ (entry − stop). The gap is what one unit can lose.

lessons.title: Stops and risk
lessons.description: Know the loss you accept before the trade begins.

exercises.prompt: What is the purpose of a stop-loss?

options.text: To cap the loss on a losing trade
To guarantee profit
To predict the next candle

exercises.explanation: A stop defines the cost of being wrong, so one trade cannot sink the account.

exercises.prompt: You entered at 100 with a stop at 95. Which candle would trigger it?

options.text: Candle 1
Candle 2

exercises.explanation: Candle 2 trades down to 94, below the 95 stop.

exercises.prompt: Complete the stop rule.
exercises.explanation: The stop converts an unknown loss into a known one.

exercises.prompt: What is the disciplined choice?
exercises.body: Price is approaching your stop. You move the stop lower so you do not have to take the loss.

options.text: Keep moving the stop
Accept the stop you planned

exercises.explanation: Moving a stop turns a planned loss into an unplanned one.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: A stop-loss order guarantees your exit price in every market.
exercises.explanation: Prices can gap past a stop, so the fill may be worse. A stop limits the loss but does not fix the price.

exercises.prompt: Match each order with what it does.

right.text: Exits at a set loss level
Exits at a set gain level

exercises.explanation: One order caps the loss and the other locks in a target gain.

exercises.prompt: Which candle traded down to a stop placed at 188?

options.text: Candle 1
Candle 2
Candle 3

exercises.explanation: Candle 2 traded down to 186, through the 188 stop. The other candles never reached that level.

exercises.prompt: A trader moves a stop farther from entry after the trade goes against them. Why is this risky?

options.text: It increases the loss they agreed to accept
It locks in a profit
It removes all risk

exercises.explanation: Moving the stop after entry changes the risk plan mid-trade, and the loss grows beyond the original limit.

lessons.title: Spotting scams
lessons.description: Urgency, guarantees, and requests for crypto.

exercises.prompt: Tap every red flag in this message.

artifact.title: Message from @hodlo_support_team
artifact.body: Hey! Your wallet is flagged. I can double your BTC in 30 minutes, guaranteed. Send 0.1 BTC to bc1q-example-address before your account closes.

exercises.explanation: Urgency, guaranteed profit, and a request to send crypto are the three classic markers.

exercises.prompt: Which offer is the clearest red flag?

options.text: A guaranteed 10x in a week
A fee schedule on a public exchange
A risk disclosure document

exercises.explanation: Nobody can guarantee returns. A guarantee is the tell.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: Support staff may ask for your seed phrase to verify your account.
exercises.explanation: No support process needs a seed phrase. Anyone asking is trying to take the funds.

exercises.prompt: Match each tactic with what it is really doing.
exercises.explanation: Both shortcuts skip the verification a real opportunity would survive.

exercises.prompt: Tap every red flag in this message.

artifact.title: Message from @exchange_support
artifact.body: Your account is locked. Verify now by entering your login and 2FA code on this link, or the account is closed today.

exercises.explanation: Urgency and a request for login codes are classic phishing markers. Real support never asks for them.

exercises.prompt: A stranger from a dating app sends you a trading app they set up for you. What do you do?

options.text: Refuse and do not install it
Install it and deposit a small test amount
Share your password so they can help

exercises.explanation: Apps set up by strangers are a common way to steal deposits. Any test amount is already a loss.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: A celebrity endorsing a coin proves the coin is legitimate.
exercises.explanation: Endorsements can be bought or faked. Check the project through independent sources.

exercises.prompt: Put these steps in order when you suspect a scam.

steps.text: Stop replying and do not click any links
Check the official site or app directly
Report the account to the platform

exercises.explanation: End contact first, verify through a channel you already trust, then report.

lessons.title: Seed phrase safety
lessons.description: The one secret nobody legitimate will ask for.

exercises.prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

artifact.title: Wallet verification required
artifact.body: We detected unusual activity. Reply with your 12-word recovery phrase within 24 hours or your funds will be frozen. Do not contact support through the app.

hotspots.label: Blocking official channels
hotspots.text: Do not contact support through the app

exercises.explanation: Requests for the phrase, a tight deadline, and steering you away from official support all point to phishing.

exercises.prompt: Where should a seed phrase be stored?

options.text: Offline, in a place only you control
In a cloud note so you never lose it
In a DM with a friend

exercises.explanation: Offline and private. Cloud notes and messages are one breach away from theft.

exercises.prompt: Put a safe recovery in order.

steps.text: Get your offline backup
Open the wallet app you already use
Enter the phrase inside the app

exercises.explanation: The phrase goes into the wallet app, never into a website or a chat.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule.
parts: Never type your seed phrase into a
exercises.explanation: A website asking for your seed phrase is stealing it.

exercises.prompt: True or false?
exercises.statement: A support agent may ask for your seed phrase to verify your identity.
exercises.explanation: Legitimate support never needs your seed phrase. Anyone who asks is trying to take your funds.

exercises.prompt: Where is the safest place to keep a seed phrase?

options.text: A photo in your cloud drive
Written on paper and kept in a secure location
In a message to a trusted friend

exercises.explanation: Paper kept offline is not reachable by hackers over the internet.

exercises.prompt: Match each secret with what it protects.

right.text: Full access to the funds, with no reset option
One online account, which can usually be reset

exercises.explanation: Anyone with the seed phrase can move the funds. A password can usually be reset through the service.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about requests for your seed phrase.
parts: If someone asks for your seed phrase, treat them as a
exercises.explanation: Assume bad intent and walk away. No real service needs the phrase.
